evidence_quotes.quote: This study reviews the status of access to water supply, sanitation, and solid waste management (SWM) services in Uganda, examining the influence of national government policies, institutional frameworks, and financing mechanisms.
Funding mechanisms and resource allocation play a crucial role in determining the success of water supply, sanitation, and SWM services.
Unequal resource allocation, where water supply dominates funding whereas sanitation and SWM remain underfunded, exacerbates service delivery gaps, particularly amid rapid urbanization.
These experts came from MWE, the private sector, NGOs, and DPs. Interviews involved semistructured questions, allowing flexibility to probe deeper into specific themes.
Percentage access to water, sanitation, and SWM services in relation to population growth rates (source: World bank, AfDB, MWE, UNICEF, JICA, and KCCA).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines national water supply and sanitation service access and delivery alongside solid waste management across urban, small-town, and rural areas in Uganda.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (yes) because it examines national government and development partner policies, institutional mandates, decentralization, and sector financing frameworks. However, it fails the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading (no -> E03) because it examines high-level macro-governance background, inter-ministerial mandate overlap, policy sector counts, and aggregate donor/national budget shares across sectors rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, frontline discretion, enforcement at the access interface, or utility regulatory structure directly governing access).
criterion_notes.c3: Employs a mixed-methods sector review combining a PRISMA-guided document review of 65 policy and sector performance documents (screened from 385 records), 10 semi-structured key informant interviews analyzed in Atlas.ti, and secondary national budget and service-coverage series.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports aggregate national percentage access to water supply and sanitation services over time (1995-2023 in Figure 3, plus national coverage statistics in text) alongside institutional and policy ratings.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the unit of analysis and sample at the national/sector level in Uganda (15 sector institutions, 14 legal/policy instruments, 10 key informants from MWE, private sector, NGOs, and development partners, and national coverage/budget time series), the macro-governance/financing exposure, national coverage outcomes, and a mixed-methods document review plus key informant interview design.

study_design: Mixed-methods sector review combining structured document/policy review (65 documents), qualitative key informant interviews (n = 10), and descriptive secondary analysis of national budget and coverage data
population_and_sample: National water, sanitation, and solid waste management sector in Uganda (unit of analysis: sector institutions, policies, and national population aggregates; 65 reviewed policy/performance documents, 15 rated institutions, 14 rated statutes/ordinances, and 10 purposefully selected sector key informants from MWE, private sector, NGOs, and development partners).
exposure: Macro-level national government and development partner policies, inter-ministerial institutional mandates/coordination frameworks, and aggregate sectoral budget/donor funding allocations across water, sanitation, and solid waste management.
outcome: National percentage access to water supply, sanitation, and solid waste management services (1995-2023) and qualitative/ordinal sector assessments of institutional involvement (1-5 scale) and policy coverage.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although the study examines Ugandan water and sanitation service coverage using a review of 65 documents, 10 key informant interviews, and secondary budget/coverage data (and would therefore be included under the broad plain wording of Criterion 2), its analytical focus is broad macro-governance background—specifically aggregate funding shares between water (>80%), sanitation (~5%), and solid waste management (~10%), overlapping ministerial mandates, and broad counts/ratings of national statutes—rather than an empirical analysis of a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access.
